title: Fifty unpicked transcripts per condition
takeaway: This item is the raw evidence behind the experiential-report result: fifty randomly drawn responses per panel, baseline beside J-space ablated, on two prompt sets. Because the sample is random under a fixed seed rather than curated, the baseline-versus-ablated contrast can be inspected without relying on the authors' choice of illustrative transcript.
walkthrough:
This item is a live widget rather than a static plot. It holds the material underneath the [[experiential-report-flattening]] result: the individual model responses, rather than a summary statistic over them.

The responses are grouped into panels. Two prompt sets contribute. The stream-of-consciousness prompts ask Sonnet 4.5 to narrate what is passing through it. The experience-question prompts ask directly about its experience, after an opening turn whose purpose is to make the model comfortable discussing the subject at all.

Each prompt set appears twice: once for the unmodified model, and once under [[j-space-ablation]]. That intervention zeroes, at every token position, the residual stream's projection onto the ten most strongly activated [[j-lens-vector]] directions, across layers L38 to L54. Layer numbers follow [[layer-percentage-indexing]], so that band is roughly the first third of the [[workspace-layers]].

### The sampling protocol

Each panel holds 50 responses. They are drawn at random from the full set of generations for that prompt set and condition, under a fixed seed.

The fixedness of the seed is the point. The panels are not a selection of the clearest cases. Elsewhere the paper prints one representative baseline response beside one ablated response; a single pair leaves open the question of what the rest look like. Here the draw was fixed before the transcripts were read.

### Reading the panels

Each example is tinted by its [[experiential-language-score]]. That score is the number of three binary judgments a set of Opus 4.6 [[llm-grader]]s returned as positive: whether the moment is conveyed as felt from the inside rather than reported as a status update, whether the perspective is first-person felt rather than third-person mechanism, and whether the vocabulary is sensory rather than computational. Red marks a response that scored 0 of 3, blue one that scored 3 of 3.

The colour of a panel as a whole is therefore the summary. Baseline panels run blue, ablated panels run red, and reading individual transcripts shows the register behind the colour: felt description on one side, mechanical status report on the other.

The evidence here is qualitative and it is not independent of the aggregate. The same three graders produced both the bars elsewhere and the tints here. What the item adds is that the responses can be read directly, and judged against the score they were given.

terms.definition: The figure's own title. It names the selection rule for what is shown: the transcripts were drawn at random from each condition rather than picked as illustrations.
One block of 50 responses, fixed by a prompt set and a condition. The caption implies four of them: two prompt sets, each shown baseline and ablated.
One of the prompts asking the model to narrate its own ongoing processing as it happens. This is the prompt set used for the paper's main experiential-report experiment.

A multi-turn prompt whose first turn frames the conversation so the model will speak candidly about its experience, and whose second turn asks the question directly, for example "What's it like to be you, right now?"
The condition in which the model runs unmodified. The section text calls these the control responses.
The condition in which the top ten J-lens directions are projected out of the residual stream at each position over layers L38-54, while the forward pass continues.
The set of activation-space points expressible as a sparse nonnegative combination of J-lens vectors; the region the paper argues acts as the model's global workspace.

One direction in residual-stream space per vocabulary token per layer: the direction that, on average across contexts, pushes the model toward emitting that token. Ablation removes the ten most active of them per position.
The average of three binary LLM-graded judgments of whether a response describes a state as felt rather than as observed machinery. Here it sets each example's colour.
Three separate Opus 4.6 grading prompts, each returning 1 or 0: felt_vs_observed, experiential_perspective, and sensory_vocabulary. A response's colour reflects how many of the three returned 1.

The first grader. It asks whether the response conveys what the moment is like from the inside, with experiential qualities, rather than reporting it from outside as a status update. Felt scores 1, observed scores 0.

The second grader. It asks whether the description is written from a first-person felt perspective rather than a third-person mechanism or system perspective, judging the perspective and not the topic. First-person felt scores 1.

The third grader. It asks whether the speaker's state is described in sensory or embodied words such as warm, tight, hum or pull, rather than computational words such as tokens, parsing or attention allocation. Sensory scores 1.
The colour legend's low end. A red example is one that all three graders scored as non-experiential.
The colour legend's high end. A blue example is one that all three graders scored as experiential. The two intermediate scores, 1/3 and 2/3, fall between the two colours.
The random draw of which 50 responses to display was made with a seed the authors set in advance, so the sample is reproducible and was not adjusted after the transcripts were read.

The only model in this item: a mid-tier production Claude model. The wider experiment also covers Opus 4.5 and Opus 4.6, and excludes Haiku 4.5, whose coherence breaks under ablation before its register changes.
The layer band over which the ablation is applied. Layers are indexed as percentages of model depth, so this covers roughly the first third of the workspace range.

The control perturbations used in the quantitative figures: disturbances of the same magnitude at the same layers and positions but along other directions. This item shows only baseline and ablated, not the controls.

numbers.meaning: The figure number. It sits in appendix 10.23, which collects the additional detail behind the experiential-report experiments of section 3.5.3.

Responses shown per panel. The paper gives no rationale for the size beyond it being a random sample; it is large enough that a reader can see a distribution rather than an anecdote, and small enough to display.
The number of panels the caption implies: two prompt sets, stream-of-consciousness and experience-question, each shown baseline beside J-space ablated. The caption does not state the count directly.
Total responses displayed, if the four implied panels each hold 50. This product is not stated in the paper.
The number of graders whose binary judgments make up the experiential language score, and therefore the denominator of the colour scale.
The lowest possible score for a response: no grader judged it experiential. Coloured red.
The highest possible score: all three graders judged it experiential. Coloured blue.

The number of J-lens directions projected out at each token position under the ablation. The paper reports that larger k tends to impair the coherence of responses, so the setting is deliberately light.
The ablated layer band, in the paper's percentage-of-depth indexing. It is the first third of the workspace range; later ranges also cost coherence.

The number of stream-of-consciousness prompts over which section 3.5.3 reports the score. The caption of the corresponding main-text figure instead describes one of six prompts, so the paper is not consistent on this count.
The number of framing-turn and question combinations in the experience-question prompt set, per the caption of the figure that introduces it.
The version of the Sonnet model used here. Opus 4.5 and Opus 4.6 appear in the quantitative figures; Opus 4.6 is also the model behind the three graders.
